newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Campaigning starts in Africa for U.N. post.
newsitem.headline: Campaigning starts in Africa for U.N. post.

text.p: African heads of state have started pushing their candidates for the coveted post of U.N. secretary-general after Boutros Boutros-Ghali temporarily put aside his bid for re-election in the face of a U.S. veto.

Ghana, Ivory Coast, Niger and Mauritania have formally nominated nationals as candidates and other names are likely to follow before or after Monday, when the Security Council is expected to take an informal poll on levels of support.

Organisation of African Unity Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim of Tanzania, widely tipped as a likely contender, was in the West African state of Togo on Sunday for talks with veteran Francophone President Gnassingbe Eyadema.
"What is certain is that Africa has the right to a second term as U.N. secretary-general," Salim told Togo's state television, saying some African leaders had asked him to stand.

The OAU, which threw its weight behind Egypt's Boutros-Ghali at its annual summit in Cameroon in July, threw the door open to other Africans when he set aside his candidacy last Wednesday after a November 19 U.S. veto in the Security Council blocked his path to the now traditional second term.
But while the United States opposes Boutros-Ghali, whose five-year term expires on December 31 and who reserves the right to rejoin the race, it left the door open for other Africans.
Nominees so far declared are as follows:

-- Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping. He has held a variety of top-level U.N. posts and maintained a diplomatic silence while his boss Boutros-Ghali was still in the running.
-- Ahmedou Ould Abdallah of Mauritania, former U.N. special representative for Burundi and now a co-chairman of the Global Coalition for Africa group in Washington.
-- Hamid Algabid of Niger, the secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference.
-- Amara Essy of Ivory Coast. Ivorian foreign minister and the U.N. General Assembly president in 1994-95. He brokered a peace agreement ending five years of civil war in Sierre Leone.

Ghana President Jerry Rawlings, seeking a fresh mandate in national elections on Saturday, described Annan as an "extremely competent" person. "I hope my colleagues will consider his credentials when they are making their choice," he said.
Niger's Algabid never disguised his ambition even when African states were, in theory, united behind Boutros-Ghali. He circulated a colourful curriculum vitae at July's OAU summit.

Ivorian President Henri Konan Bedie says he expects Essy to win wide support plus the backing of former colonial ruler France, a permanent Security Council member. "Ivory Coast has only friends in the world. And we will present him so that he is accepted by all," he told state television.
Diplomats expect more names to emerge, including the OAU's Salim and possibly Olara Ottunu, president of the New York-based International Peace Academy.

Senegal's foreign minister, Moustapha Niasse, and Gambia's Wally N'Dow, assistant secretary-general in charge of the Centre for Human Settlements in Nairobi, are other possible candidates but their countries ties with Taiwan make them liable to a veto from China, which considers Taiwan a rebel province.

Senegalese President Abdou Diouf backs Niasse's candidacy. "I see in him the profile of a secretary-general of the United Nations and I have given my endorsement," he said on Friday on his return from a Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso.
